newsitem.title: GERMANY: DWS-Equity funds strongest performers in 1996.
newsitem.headline: DWS-Equity funds strongest performers in 1996.

text.p: Share funds led the field among global securities-backed funds last year, with investors investing 22 percent more in equity funds than in 1995, a survey by German fund management giant DWS said on Monday.
Altogether the world's investors put around 40 percent more in equity funds in 1996, investing a total of 3.8 trillion marks in share-backed funds.

"The total amount invested in securities-backed funds in 1996 increased by 22 percent to almost nine trillion marks, with equity funds increasing their market share in most countries, with the notable exception of Japan," DWS said in the survey.

DWS, the fund management unit of Germany's largest commercial bank, Deutsche Bank, said its survey showed that the main impact behind the increase in equity-backed funds came from the United States, where the amount invested in equity funds grew 38 percent to 1.75 trillion marks.

Around 221 billion dollars of the investments in share-backed funds was composed of new investments and a large percentage of the amount invested in equity-backed funds was earmarked for pension provision.
"Growth in this area was strengthened by the fact that the so-called "Baby-Boomer" generation has only around a decade to go until it enters its pension phase," DWS said.
The amount invested in managed funds in European markets grew across the board, the survey said, but individual private pension provision played only a secondary role in increasing growth rates.
However, a gradual realisation of the need for private pension provision in European countries had a boosting effect on the amounts invested in equity funds, the survey said.

Funds saw above average growth dynamic in Belgium, Austria, Sweden, Spain and Germany in 1996. The most-dynamic level of growth was seen in Spain, where the amount under management in all kinds of investment funds grew by 57 percent.
Growth was slower in France, Switzerland and Italy because a relatively late start in the strong rise in their respective stock markets.
In Switzerland and Italy new liquidity was mainly channeled into bond-based and money-market funds.
In Italy changes from direct investment vehicles into bond and money-market funds was the cause for the slow-down and in early 1997 equity funds were again seeing a rise in investment there.

Seen over five years, the amount invested in funds has almost doubled since 1991. DWS said in the survey that the amount invested in funds, especially share funds, would increase in coming years as the need for private pension provision became The impetus for this change was coming from the United States and Britain.
